course: Small Machines & Pharmaceuticals: The Complete Import Business

lessons.title: The Documents You Need for Every Shipment
lessons.body: Every import shipment into Africa requires a core set of documents. Missing one can delay your goods for weeks and cost you demurrage fees of $50-$200 per day. The essential documents are: a Commercial Invoice, Packing List, Bill of Lading (for sea) or Air Waybill (for air), Certificate of Origin, and an Import Declaration (like the ID in Nigeria or the IDF in Kenya). For pharmaceuticals, you also need a Drug Registration Certificate and an Import Permit from the national drug regulator, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria or PPB in Kenya. For machines, you may need a Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) certificate from an inspection company like SGS or Bureau Veritas. Always prepare three original copies of each document: one for customs, one for your clearing agent, and one for your records. In Africa, many borders now use electronic systems like the Single Window in Ghana or the Tradenet in South Africa. You must upload scanned copies before the ship arrives. A common mistake is sending original documents by regular mail; use DHL or FedEx to ensure tracking and speed. Also, check that the names and addresses on all documents match exactly. A mismatch between the invoice and the bill of lading will trigger a customs query and cost you at least $100 in amendment fees. Start by creating a checklist for each shipment and tick off every document before the cargo leaves the supplier.

lessons.title: Commercial Invoice and Packing List
lessons.body: The Commercial Invoice is the seller's bill to you. It must show: seller and buyer names and addresses, invoice number and date, detailed description of goods (including brand, model, and serial numbers for machines), quantity, unit price, total value, currency (usually USD), Incoterms (like FOB or CIF), and country of origin. For pharmaceuticals, include batch numbers and expiry dates. Customs uses this to calculate duty. Under-declaring value to pay less duty is illegal and can lead to seizure and fines of 50% of the goods' value. The Packing List shows how goods are packed: number of cartons, weight per carton, dimensions, and contents of each package. It helps customs officers locate items for inspection. For machines, list each component separately. For pharmaceuticals, list each drug, strength, and quantity per box. Both documents must be in English or the official language of the destination country. Use a spreadsheet to create these documents; templates are available from trade portals like the International Trade Centre's TradeMap. Always keep digital and hard copies. When you send them to your clearing agent, use PDF format to prevent editing. A common error is using generic descriptions like 'spare parts' or 'medicine' â be specific: '10 units of Bosch GWS 20-180 angle grinder, 180mm, 2000W' or '500 boxes of Coartem 20/120mg tablets, 6x4 tablets per box'. Specificity speeds up clearance and reduces the chance of customs asking for a physical inspection, which can add 3-5 days.

lessons.title: Bill of Lading and Air Waybill
lessons.body: The Bill of Lading (B/L) is a contract between the shipper and the shipping line. It serves as a receipt, a document of title, and a contract of carriage. For sea freight, you need an Original B/L or a Telex Release. The Original B/L must be endorsed by the shipper and presented to the shipping line to collect your cargo. A Telex Release is faster: the shipper surrenders the original at origin, and you get a release at destination. Always confirm with your supplier which type they will provide. The B/L shows: shipper, consignee (you or your clearing agent), notify party, vessel name, port of loading, port of discharge, container number, seal number, and description of goods. Check that the consignee name matches your import license exactly. For air freight, the Air Waybill (AWB) is not a document of title; it is a receipt and contract. The airline releases cargo to the consignee named on the AWB without requiring an original document. This makes air freight faster but riskier if you have not paid your supplier. Always use a freight forwarder to handle B/L and AWB. In Africa, major ports like Mombasa, Lagos, and Durban have online systems to track containers. For example, in Kenya, you can use the Kenya Ports Authority's online portal. If your B/L is delayed, you can request a Letter of Indemnity from your bank, but this costs 1-2% of the cargo value. Keep all B/L and AWB copies for at least 5 years for tax audits.

lessons.title: Certificate of Origin
lessons.body: The Certificate of Origin (COO) proves where your goods were manufactured. It is essential for customs to determine duty rates under trade agreements. For example, under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), goods originating in member countries may enjoy reduced or zero tariffs. To benefit, you need a valid COO from a recognized chamber of commerce or customs authority in the exporting country. For machines from China, you need a COO issued by the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT). For pharmaceuticals from India, a COO from the Indian Chamber of Commerce. The COO must show: exporter, consignee, country of origin, description of goods, and a declaration signed by the exporter and stamped by the issuing authority. Some countries require a legalized COO from their embassy in the exporting country; this costs about $50-$100 and takes 3-5 days. In Africa, many customs authorities now accept electronic COOs through the ASYCUDA World system. However, always carry a hard copy. A wrong or missing COO can result in you paying the full general duty rate, which can be 20-35% instead of 0-10%. For example, a machine classified under HS code 8467 (tools) may have a 5% duty with a COO from a trade partner, but 20% without. Always verify the HS code with your customs agent before shipment. Also, check if your country has a specific form, like the EUR.1 for European goods or the Form A for GSP. Keep the COO with your customs file.

lessons.title: Import Permits and Licenses
lessons.body: Before you import, you must obtain the necessary permits and licenses. For general goods, you need an Import License or Importer Registration Certificate from your country's customs authority. In Nigeria, this is the Form M and the Importers Certificate. In Kenya, it is the Import Declaration Form (IDF) and a PIN certificate. For pharmaceuticals, you need a Drug Import Permit from the national drug regulator: NAFDAC in Nigeria, PPB in Kenya, FDA in Ghana, or SAHPRA in South Africa. This permit requires you to submit the product's Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (CPP), GMP certificate, and samples for testing. The process takes 2-6 weeks and costs $200-$1000 per product. For machines, some countries require a Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) from agencies like SGS, Intertek, or Bureau Veritas. This inspection happens in the exporting country and costs 0.5-1% of the FOB value. You also need a Tax Identification Number (TIN) and sometimes a customs bond. For controlled goods like generators or used machines, you may need an environmental permit. Always check with your clearing agent before you order. A common mistake is importing without a permit, leading to seizure and fines. For example, importing pharmaceuticals without a NAFDAC permit in Nigeria can result in destruction of goods and a fine of â¦5 million. Start the permit process early: 8-12 weeks before shipment. Use online portals like the Nigeria Single Window or Kenya TradeNet to apply. Keep digital copies and renew annually.

lessons.title: Working with Customs Clearing Agents
lessons.body: A customs clearing agent is your local expert who handles documentation, duty payment, and cargo release. In Africa, you cannot clear cargo yourself at most ports; you must use a licensed agent. Choose an agent with a proven track record and a customs license. Ask for referrals from other importers. Fees vary: in Nigeria, agents charge 2-5% of the CIF value or a flat fee of $200-$500 per container. In Kenya, KES 20,000-50,000. Always sign a written contract specifying duties, timelines, and penalties for delays. Provide your agent with all documents at least 5 days before arrival. Your agent will submit the customs declaration, pay duties on your behalf, and arrange inspection. For pharmaceuticals, ensure the agent has experience with NAFDAC or PPB. For machines, they should know HS codes and duty rates. A good agent will advise you on duty optimization, like using the correct HS code or claiming exemptions. Avoid agents who ask for cash without receipts; always pay through bank transfer for traceability. After clearance, get a copy of the Bill of Lading, Customs Release, and Duty Payment Receipt. Keep these for your records. If you have a dispute, contact the customs authority directly. In many countries, you can track your clearance online using the customs portal. For example, in Ghana, use the ICUMS system; in South Africa, the SARS eFiling. Build a long-term relationship with one reliable agent to get better rates and faster service. Never use an agent who promises to undervalue goods; it is illegal and risky.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Customs Clearance and Documentation

In the import business, your paperwork is your product. A container of small machines or a pharmaceutical consignment can sit at Mombasa, Tema, or Durban for weeks â accruing demurrage, storage, and penalties â because one document is missing, mismatched, or unsigned. This reference lesson gives you the exact documents, the data they must contain, and the working habits that get cargo released fast and legally. Treat it as your desktop manual.

Why documentation drives the business

Customs authorities in Africa operate on a risk-management model: they assess your declaration, compare it against the documents, and decide whether to release, inspect, or detain. When documents agree with each other and with the physical cargo, you are a low-risk trader and clear quickly. When they conflict â a weight that doesn't match the packing list, an invoice value below the customs reference price, a certificate of origin that doesn't match the invoice â you become a high-risk trader and every subsequent shipment faces scrutiny. Documentation accuracy is therefore a commercial strategy, not a clerical chore.

The core document set

Every commercial import requires a minimum set. Which specific documents apply depends on the product, the origin, and the destination country.

Getting the details right: invoice and packing list

The commercial invoice is the customs valuation document. It must show: seller and buyer full legal names and addresses; invoice number and date; description of goods in plain language (not just a model code); quantity, unit price, and total value in the invoice currency; Incoterms (e.g. FOB, CIF); country of origin; and payment terms. Customs uses this to determine the customs value, which is usually CIF (cost, insurance, freight) for African ports. Under-declaring to save duty is the single most common cause of detention, fines, and seizure â and it destroys your credibility for future shipments.

The packing list is the physical description document. It must show: number of packages; type of packaging (cartons, pallets, crates); net and gross weight; dimensions; and the contents of each package. For small machines, list each unit's serial number where available. For pharmaceuticals, list batch numbers, manufacturing and expiry dates, and dosage form. This is the document customs uses to verify that what was declared is what actually arrived.

Table 1: Minimum data on invoice and packing list (Africa import context)
Field Commercial Invoice Packing List
Seller / buyer legal names & addressesRequiredRequired
Invoice number & dateRequiredOptional (cross-ref)
Full goods descriptionRequiredRequired
Quantity, unit price, total valueRequiredNot required
Incoterms & currencyRequiredNot required
Country of originRequiredOptional
Number & type of packagesOptionalRequired
Net & gross weightOptionalRequired
Batch / serial numbersOptionalRequired (machines, pharma)
Manufacturing / expiry datesOptionalRequired (pharma)

Source: compiled from WCO HS Convention guidance and national customs documentation requirements (Kenya Revenue Authority, Ghana Revenue Authority, Nigeria Customs Service).

Transport documents: bill of lading and air waybill

The bill of lading (B/L) is issued by the shipping line for sea freight. It is a receipt, a contract of carriage, and â critically â a document of title. Whoever holds the original B/L can claim the goods. For imports into Africa, you will usually deal with an original B/L, a telex release, or a sea waybill. The B/L must show: shipper, consignee, notify party, port of loading and discharge, vessel and voyage, container and seal numbers, description of goods, number of packages, gross weight, freight terms (prepaid/collect), and the number of original B/Ls issued.

The air waybill (AWB) is issued by the airline or freight forwarder for air freight. It is a receipt and contract of carriage but not a document of title â the consignee named on the AWB can usually collect the goods on arrival. The AWB must show: shipper, consignee, airport of departure and destination, flight details, pieces, weight, chargeable weight, declared value for carriage and customs, and handling information. For high-value small machines and pharmaceuticals, air freight is common and the AWB is your key release document.

Certificate of origin

The certificate of origin (COO) proves where the goods were produced. It matters commercially because it determines eligibility for preferential tariff rates under trade agreements such as the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the COMESA Free Trade Area, the SADC Protocol on Trade, or the EUâAfrica Economic Partnership Agreements. A COO issued by an authorised body â a chamber of commerce, a customs authority, or a designated export promotion agency â can reduce or eliminate duty. An incorrect or missing COO means you pay the full Most-Favoured-Nation rate. For AfCFTA, the rules of origin are product-specific, so confirm the applicable rule before you ship.

Import permits and licences

Many products cannot be imported into African countries without a prior permit or licence. Pharmaceuticals and medical devices are the classic case: they typically require registration with the national medicines regulator (e.g. NAFDAC in Nigeria, Pharmacy and Poisons Board in Kenya, Ghana FDA, SAHPRA in South Africa) and an import permit. Small machines may require standards conformity (e.g. KEBS in Kenya, SON in Nigeria, Ghana Standards Authority) or energy/telecom approvals. Other controlled categories include food, cosmetics, chemicals, used goods, and items subject to quota. The practical rule: check the destination country's prohibited and restricted goods list before you place the order, not after the container arrives.

â  SAFETY AND LEGAL WARNING â PHARMACEUTICALS

Importing pharmaceuticals without a valid product registration and import permit is a criminal offence in most African jurisdictions and can result in seizure, destruction of the consignment, fines, and imprisonment. Counterfeit, substandard, or unregistered medicines endanger patients and expose you to product liability. Never import medicines through informal channels or without confirming the destination regulator's requirements in writing. For small machines, ensure electrical and safety conformity â non-compliant equipment can cause fire, injury, or fatality and will be rejected at port.

Working with customs clearing agents

A licensed customs clearing agent (also called a freight forwarder or customs broker) is your operational partner at the port. In most African countries, only licensed agents can lodge declarations in the customs system. A good agent does more than file: they pre-classify your goods, advise on duty and tax, arrange inspection, manage the terminal and shipping line, and flag problems before they become demurrage. A bad agent under-declares, misses deadlines, or disappears with your documents.

Choose an agent with: a current licence from the customs authority; a physical office at or near the port; references from importers of similar goods; transparent fee structure; and a track record with your product category (pharma and machinery require different expertise). Agree on a written scope: who pays duty and taxes, who handles inspection, who bears demurrage if delays occur, and how documents are returned. Keep digital and physical copies of every document you hand over.

Table 2: Document checklist by shipment type (Africa import)
Document Small Machines (sea/air) Pharmaceuticals (air/sea)
Commercial invoiceRequiredRequired
Packing listRequiredRequired
Bill of lading / air waybillRequiredRequired
Certificate of originRequired (for preference)Required (for preference)
Import permit / licenceSometimes (standards, energy)Always (regulator + permit)
Product registration certificateNot usuallyRequired (e.g. NAFDAC, PPB, FDA)
Certificate of analysis / batch recordsNot usuallyRequired
Insurance certificateRequired if CIFRequired if CIF
Import declaration (single window)RequiredRequired
Tax identification / importer registrationRequiredRequired

Source: compiled from national customs and regulator requirements â Kenya Revenue Authority, Pharmacy and Poisons Board (Kenya), NAFDAC (Nigeria), Ghana FDA, SAHPRA (South Africa).

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm the destination country's restricted goods list before ordering â permits and registrations take time.
  2. Match every document: names, addresses, descriptions, quantities, weights, and values must agree across invoice, packing list, B/L or AWB, and declaration.
  3. Declare the true customs value using the correct Incoterm â under-declaration is the fastest route to fines and seizure.
  4. Secure the original B/L or telex release before the vessel arrives; without it you cannot collect sea freight.
  5. Obtain a valid certificate of origin and confirm the AfCFTA, COMESA, or SADC rule of origin for your product.
  6. For pharmaceuticals, verify product registration and import permit with the national regulator in writing.
  7. Appoint a licensed, referenced clearing agent with a written scope covering duty, inspection, demurrage, and document return.
  8. Keep digital and physical copies of every document for at least five years for audit and future shipments.

Further Reading (free official sources)

  • World Customs Organization â Trade Tools and HS classification
  • African Union â AfCFTA official portal (rules of origin, tariff schedules)
  • Kenya Revenue Authority â Customs and TradeNet documentation
  • Ghana Revenue Authority â ICUMS and customs procedures
  • Nigeria Customs Service â import procedures and Trade Hub

Disclaimer: Requirements change frequently. Always verify current documentation and permit requirements with the destination country's customs authority and product regulator before shipping.

quiz.q: Which document is NOT required for every import shipment?
quiz.explanation: Certificate of Origin is not always required for every shipment; it depends on trade agreements and destination country rules.

quiz.q: What is the penalty for under-declaring the value of goods on a Commercial Invoice?
options: B) 50% of goods' value as fine
quiz.explanation: Under-declaring is illegal and can lead to seizure and fines of 50% of the goods' value.

quiz.q: Which document serves as a document of title for sea freight?
quiz.explanation: The Bill of Lading is a document of title, allowing the holder to claim the goods.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a Certificate of Origin?
options: B) To determine duty rates under trade agreements
C) To list contents of packages
D) To act as a contract of carriage
quiz.explanation: Certificate of Origin proves where goods were manufactured, which affects duty rates under trade agreements.

quiz.q: Which agency issues a Drug Import Permit in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: NAFDAC is the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control in Nigeria.

quiz.q: What is a common fee charged by customs clearing agents in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: Agents in Nigeria typically charge 2-5% of the CIF value or a flat fee.

quiz.q: Which document is NOT a document of title?
quiz.explanation: The Air Waybill is not a document of title; it is a receipt and contract only.

quiz.q: What is the first step before importing pharmaceuticals into Kenya?
options: A) Obtain an Import Permit from PPB
quiz.explanation: You must obtain an Import Permit from the Pharmacy and Poisons Board (PPB) before importation.

quiz.q: Which system is used for customs clearance in Ghana?
quiz.explanation: Ghana uses the Integrated Customs Management System (ICUMS).

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a legalized Certificate of Origin from an embassy?
quiz.explanation: Legalization by an embassy costs about $50-$100 and takes 3-5 days.

quiz.q: Which document must match the consignee name exactly to avoid customs delays?
quiz.explanation: The consignee name on the Bill of Lading must match the import license exactly.

quiz.q: What is a Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC)?
options: B) An inspection certificate for machines
quiz.explanation: PVoC is an inspection in the exporting country to ensure goods meet standards, often required for machines.

quiz.q: How many original copies of each document should you prepare?
quiz.explanation: Three originals: one for customs, one for your agent, and one for your records.

quiz.q: Which trade agreement can reduce tariffs for goods originating in Africa?
quiz.explanation: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) reduces tariffs among member countries.

quiz.q: What is the penalty for importing pharmaceuticals without a NAFDAC permit in Nigeria?
options: B) â¦5 million fine and destruction of goods
quiz.explanation: Importing without a NAFDAC permit can lead to destruction of goods and a fine of â¦5 million.

quiz.q: Which document is used for air freight?
quiz.explanation: Air Waybill is used for air freight, while Bill of Lading is for sea freight.

quiz.q: What should you do if your Bill of Lading is delayed?
options: B) Request a Letter of Indemnity from your bank
quiz.explanation: A Letter of Indemnity from your bank can be used, but it costs 1-2% of cargo value.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common mistake on a Commercial Invoice?
quiz.explanation: Generic descriptions like 'spare parts' can cause customs delays; be specific.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a Drug Import Permit?
quiz.explanation: Drug Import Permits typically cost $200-$1000 per product.

quiz.q: Which online system is used for customs in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Kenya uses the Kenya TradeNet System for customs clearance.

quiz.q: What is the role of a customs clearing agent?
options: B) To handle documentation and cargo release
quiz.explanation: A clearing agent handles customs documentation, duty payment, and cargo release.

quiz.q: Which document shows the contents of each package?
quiz.explanation: The Packing List details the contents, weight, and dimensions of each package.

quiz.q: What is the HS code used for?
quiz.explanation: HS codes classify goods to determine applicable duty rates.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a required document for pharmaceuticals?
quiz.explanation: Certificate of Origin is not specific to pharmaceuticals; it may be required for all goods but not unique.

quiz.q: What is a Telex Release?
options: A) A type of Bill of Lading
B) A release of cargo without original B/L
quiz.explanation: A Telex Release allows cargo release without the original Bill of Lading.

quiz.q: Which agency issues a Certificate of Origin in China?
quiz.explanation: The China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT) issues COOs in China.

quiz.q: What is the typical demurrage fee per day for delayed cargo?
quiz.explanation: Demurrage fees can range from $50-$200 per day, depending on the port.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using an agent who promises to undervalue goods?
options: A) It is illegal and risky
D) It is not allowed by banks
quiz.explanation: Undervaluing goods is illegal and can lead to seizure and fines.

quiz.q: Which document is NOT needed for customs clearance?
quiz.explanation: A Business Plan is not a customs document; the others are essential.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check on a Bill of Lading?
options: A) Consignee name matches import license
quiz.explanation: The consignee name must match your import license exactly to avoid delays.
